articles.body: Patrick Mahomes, the Kansas City Chiefs’ star player, and his wife, Brittany Mahomes, have been successful business partners for quite a while now. Ahead of the new season, it seems their investment in the NWSL team, the Kansas City Current, which has reached a valuation of $325 million has marked another multi million milestone.Patrick Mahomes and Brittany Mahomes’ Kansas City Current raises multi million dollar investment from the cityA few days ago, Patrick Mahomes and Brittany Mahomes’ Kansas City Current was successful at getting a $235 million funding package approved from the city to expand their stadium and entertainment district.For the unversed, the Kansas City Current built the stadium with their own funding and had not taken it from anywhere else. When the stadium turned out to be successful, it seems the city stepped in with funding to make it bigger.As per reports, the funding will be used to add 6,500 more seats to their stadium increasing the capacity to 18,000.But that’s not all; a parking garage will also be built and more mixed-use development in the Current Landing district.Kansas City Mayor Quinton Lucas weighed in on it as, “I think it's going to continue to help us build out the riverfront in Kansas City long term…It is impressive that you have a team that invested not only in women's sports, but in an area of the city that was underinvested largely, that they have seen this level of success and that they're continuing to see expansion long term.”The Kansas City Current’s co-owners, Angie and Chris Long,also opened up about it in a statement which read as, “Today’s decision reflects Kansas City’s belief in bold ideas and transformational projects…We are proud to continue investing in Kansas City’s future and grateful for the partnership that makes this next chapter possible.”The statement added, “The success of the Current and the Riverfront benefit our entire community, and we are honored to help create a lasting legacy for a city that has given so much to us.”While neither Patrick Mahomes nor his wife, Brittany Mahomes, reacted to it, they have remained closely associated with the Kansas City Current.Patrick Mahomes and Brittany Mahomes remain dedicated to the Kansas City CurrentFor the unversed, it was Brittany Mahomes who invested in the Kansas City Current in 2020 initially.Three years later, in 2023, the Kansas City Chiefs’ star player Patrick Mahomes followed his wife’s footsteps and also invested in the team.Both of them have often spoken about how they have remained dedicated to the NWSL team as they are often spotted cheering them on.For now, Patrick Mahomes’ focus remains on the new season as he prepares to make a comeback.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: Tom Brady, the New England Patriots’ legend, and his ex wife, Gisele Bündchen, were a power couple for over a decade until their marriage ended in 2022. While their divorce has dominated headlines, there are new remarks of Gisele Bündchen making controversial remarks about Tom Brady.Did Gisele Bündchen call out Tom Brady for “abandoning” her and their children, fur years after their high profile divorce?No, the Brazilian supermodel Gisele Bündchen has made no such remarks about the seven time Super Bowl champion, Tom Brady.A fan page took to X and made a post as, “Gisele Bündchen finally reveals why she ended her marriage to Ex husband Tom Brady over claims that he abandoned their kids and cheated on her. “Tom wasn’t there for me, especially for our kids. And I regretted everything. It got to a point where I gave Tom an ultimatum to choose between his family and his football career"”.It's a complete lie as Gisele Bündchen has only ever said good things about her ex husband, Tom Brady. articles.title: Travis Kelce’s emotional homeless charity story debunked after fake diner claims and AI-generated images emerge
articles.summary: NFL News: A heartwarming story about Travis Kelce buying a diner from his college days and turning it into a place that serves free meals to homeless people cap.
articles.body: A heartwarming story about Travis Kelce buying a diner from his college days and turning it into a place that serves free meals to homeless people captured attention online. The tale sounded like the kind of quiet act of generosity fans might expect from the NFL star. But the emotional story does not hold up. Snopes investigated the claim and found no credible evidence that the diner, its owner or the alleged charity operation ever existed.Travis Kelce diner claim had no credible evidenceThe viral story began circulating online in June 2025, with social media posts claiming Kelce had purchased a small diner that once allowed him to eat without paying immediately while he was in college.One widely shared post described the supposed transformation in striking terms: "Travis Kelce bought the tiny diner that let him eat on credit in college — but what he turned it into now feeds 120 homeless people every day."According to the story, Kelce had regularly visited a diner run by a woman named Elena. She allegedly allowed the future NFL star to keep a running tab for two years. Years later, the story claimed, Kelce found Elena after learning that she was closing the business.The supposed reunion was presented as the emotional heart of the story. Kelce allegedly bought the diner and asked Elena to return to the kitchen, this time to prepare free meals for 120 homeless people each day.It was an appealing narrative, but the details could not be independently verified.Snopes reported that searches across major search engines found no credible news reports confirming that Kelce had purchased such a business or launched a daily meal program. Searches also failed to locate Kansas City establishments called Elena's Diner or Elena's Kitchen.That absence matters. A project involving an NFL star of Kelce's profile and free meals for more than 100 people every day would likely have generated some reliable coverage.Viral Travis Kelce charity photos were also questionedThe story gained extra attention because posts included photographs that appeared to show Kelce personally serving food to people experiencing homelessness. However, those images raised another major red flag.Snopes said an AI image detection service identified the photographs as highly likely to have been generated using artificial intelligence. The images reportedly contained visual inconsistencies, including unusual eyes and an oddly formed hand.The questionable photographs added to the evidence that the story was not a genuine account of Kelce's charitable work.Snopes also found another similar story claiming Kelce had donated $50,000 to a diner that supposedly fed him as a teenager. That version was likewise presented without credible evidence.The recurring pattern is important. Inspirational celebrity stories can spread rapidly because they offer a simple emotional message: someone who received kindness eventually returned it on a much larger scale. But an uplifting story is not automatically a true one.In this case, the evidence points in the opposite direction. The viral claim that Travis Kelce bought a diner from his college days and converted it into a free meal center for homeless people is false, according to Snopes' investigation.Fans may still admire Kelce's real charitable efforts, but those should not be confused with an invented diner story simply because the narrative sounds believable.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Inspiring story on leadership: "I always define leadership as: do you care about your teammates...and do you care what we're trying to accomplish"- How Tom Brady led teams to greatness
articles.summary: NFL News: Tom Brady spent more than two decades being judged by rings, records and unforgettable performances. Yet when he talks about leadership, his definitio.
articles.body: Tom Brady spent more than two decades being judged by rings, records and unforgettable performances. Yet when he talks about leadership, his definition reaches far beyond statistics. In a discussion about motivating teammates, Brady explained why genuine care, trust and a shared purpose shaped the way he led. His words offer a revealing look at the mindset behind one of football's most successful careers.Tom Brady’s leadership philosophy was built around caringBrady's approach to leadership was not simply about demanding more from the players around him. He believed a leader first had to build a relationship with the people he expected to follow him.During the PBD Podcast, Brady discussed his leadership style and what helped him motivate teammates. The conversation, published in 2023, turned toward leadership, when host Patrick Bet-David asked Brady about the methods he used to drive his players.Brady's answer centered on one word: caring.He explained that the relationship between a leader and teammates cannot be purely transactional. Players need to believe that the person beside them genuinely cares about them and about the goal they are pursuing together.That idea also appears in Brady's later Harvard Business Review work, where he expanded on his definition of team leadership. The article, “Tom Brady on the Art of Leading Teammates,” was published in 2024 and explored seven principles he believed helped leaders bring out the best in teammates.The quote at the center of this discussion captures that philosophy:“I always define leadership as, do you care about your teammates or coworkers, and do you care what we’re trying to accomplish?” Brady. “That, to me, is great leadership. And there are a lot of people that go about those in different ways.”The wording is powerful because Brady does not begin with authority, experience or talent. He begins with people.For him, leadership starts with asking whether teammates know they matter and whether everyone remains committed to the same objective.When and where Tom Brady shared the leadership messageThe quote has circulated online in shortened form, but its underlying idea is supported by Brady's own extended comments.In the 2023 PBD Podcast conversation, Brady said his view of relationships in a team environment came down to caring about the other person and collectively caring about what the group was trying to achieve. He argued that trust develops when people know their leader genuinely cares about them.That conversation gives important context to the quote. Brady was not describing leadership as a motivational speech or a title attached to a job. He was talking about the daily relationship between teammates.He also stressed the importance of vulnerability and mutual trust. In his view, players had to feel comfortable relying on one another. That trust could not be manufactured simply because someone was the quarterback or captain.Brady's later HBR article developed the same philosophy in greater detail. He wrote that leadership comes down to caring about teammates and caring about winning together. He connected that belief to trust, arguing that people are more willing to give their best when they feel valued by those around them.Tom Brady learned team-first leadership at MichiganBrady traced much of his team-first mindset back to his time at the University of Michigan.His college career did not follow the straightforward path often associated with a future NFL superstar. He redshirted as a freshman and later found himself behind other quarterbacks on the depth chart. Yet those setbacks became part of his leadership education.In his HBR article, Brady recalled competing with Brian Griese for the starting quarterback position. Griese won the job, and Brady said his role was to support and challenge him in practice rather than undermine him. Michigan went undefeated that season and won the national championship.That experience reinforced a lesson that stayed with him.Individual recognition was not the ultimate prize. Winning as a group mattered more.Brady later described this mindset through an old sports question: whether someone wants to be a star or a champion. For him, the answer was clear. He wanted to contribute to something bigger than himself.That attitude became especially important during his NFL career. As a quarterback, Brady naturally occupied one of the most visible positions on the field. Every touchdown, mistake and major decision could draw attention to him.But he repeatedly emphasized the people around him.How Brady put his leadership philosophy into practiceBrady's definition of leadership becomes more meaningful when paired with the examples he gave from his playing career.At Tampa Bay, he noticed that screen plays were producing poor results because offensive linemen were missing blocks. Rather than simply criticizing them, Brady created his own incentive. He promised to pay each offensive lineman $1,000 whenever a screen play gained more than 15 yards.The money was not necessarily the main point. Brady believed the gesture showed appreciation and made the linemen feel involved in the outcome.He also spoke about recognizing people whose contributions were less visible. Football teams rely on trainers, equipment staff, meal workers and many others whose names rarely appear in headlines.Brady believed leaders should make those people feel valued too.His approach also involved holding teammates accountable. Because he worked to establish trust, he felt he could challenge players directly without making them feel personally attacked. That balance between support and honesty became another important part of his leadership style.Perhaps that is what makes Brady's words resonate beyond football.A quarterback can throw a perfect pass, but he cannot win alone. A business executive can set a strategy, but employees still have to believe in it. A coach can design a game plan, but players have to trust one another enough to execute it.Brady's message is therefore much bigger than his NFL career.Leadership, in his view, is not about standing above everyone else. It is about standing with them, understanding what they need and making sure everyone remains connected to the same goal.That is why his simple question carries so much weight: Do you care about your teammates, and do you care about what you are trying to accomplish together?For a player who spent his career chasing championships, Brady's answer offers a different definition of what it means to win. The scoreboard may measure the final result, but the relationships built along the way can determine whether a team ever gets there in the first place.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: How Aaron Rodgers chose love over fame and why his wife refuses to be part of the spotlight: “I have legitimate stalkers”
articles.summary: NFL News: Aaron Rodgers spent two decades as one of the most scrutinized athletes in America. Four MVP awards. A Super Bowl ring. High-profile relationships tha.
articles.body: Aaron Rodgers spent two decades as one of the most scrutinized athletes in America. Four MVP awards. A Super Bowl ring. High-profile relationships that played out, messily, in public. So when he quietly married a woman named Brittani in the spring of 2025, confirmed the wedding only after reporters spotted a ring on his finger at a Pittsburgh Steelers press conference, and then refused to show her face to the world, people noticed. Not because it was unusual for a celebrity to want privacy. Because for Rodgers, it looked like an entirely different man.Why is Aaron Rodgers keeping his wife Brittani hidden from the public?The answer, according to Aaron Rodgers himself, is deceptively simple. Brittani never asked to be famous. She has no social media presence. She did not attend a single Steelers game during the 2025 season. And Rodgers has been fiercely deliberate about keeping it that way."I had a public relationship, how did that work out?" he said on The Pat McAfee Show last June. "Now, I'm with somebody who's private, who doesn't want to be in the public eye, didn't sign up to be a celebrity, doesn't want to be a part of it."That was not a throwaway line. Rodgers had just come off a string of relationships that each, in different ways, became public spectacles. Olivia Munn. Shailene Woodley. Danica Patrick. He was engaged to Woodley, they broke it off, and the aftermath dragged on publicly for months. On the Pat McAfee Show in March 2026, Rodgers was blunt about what that era cost him. "I dealt with politically bipolar," he said, without naming anyone specifically. "I dealt with depressed relevant seeking. I dealt with people that wanted to search out other possibilities before they could commit to me. And then they go on TV talking about how I ruin their lives."He called it "crazy town." Brittani, by every indication, is the opposite of that world.Who is Brittani and why has nobody seen her yet?Aaron Rodgers first met Brittani back in 2017, though the two only recently reconnected before tying the knot. He casually revealed her first name on McAfee's show in December 2024 while talking about a Christmas package that had not arrived for his girlfriend. That was it. No last name. No photos. No Instagram tag.Since then, the curiosity has turned into something Rodgers describes as genuinely alarming. "Not just that, but stalked at the coffee shop I would frequent, the gym at ProActive that I would go to, which was really bizarre," Rodgers said. "And then the paparazzi was stalking me for a long time flying drones over my house."The situation got bad enough that he moved out of his Malibu home entirely. "We're not living at the beach anymore," he said. "Part of it is, I have legitimate stalkers, and I don't say that lightly or flippantly."This is the context that most coverage misses. The secrecy around Brittani is not a publicity strategy or a calculated mystique. It is a direct response to real safety concerns. Rodgers has been clear that her identity will be revealed only on her terms, if ever. "If and when she wants to be out, and there's a picture, she'll choose that and she has a right to that," he said.How did Brittani help Aaron Rodgers reconnect with his estranged family?This is where the story gets genuinely interesting. In August 2026, Rodgers posted photos on Instagram from a weekend in Nashville with his parents, Ed and Darla, his brother Luke, Luke's wife, and their two kids. For anyone who has followed his career, that image was startling. Rodgers had been estranged from his family for over a decade.He gave Brittani the credit, directly and without hesitation."I'm happy to be reunited, and that part of my life is a really beautiful addition," he said during an August 1 appearance on NFL Network. "And I've got to give my wife a lot of credit for -- not that she was pushing me, because she never was, but just the way that she loves and supports me.""Having those conversations with my wife allowed me to open up to the possibility of coming together," Rodgers said. "It's been a couple-year process now, the conversations with them. I've been very closed off about that part of my life, and I want to keep it that way. But there's been a narrative that's gone on for too long that I wanted to shut down, and it's been really beautiful to reconnect with them. All of them.""I got to spend a long weekend recently. I got to be an uncle. It's just really special. So a lot of my life has been full circle," he added.For a man who built his career on controlled aggression and sharp reads under pressure, this is a different kind of revelation. Not the ring. Not the secret ceremony. But the idea that the woman he married quietly, away from cameras, was the one who helped him find his way back to a family he had shut out for years.Rodgers has confirmed the 2026 season will be his last. When it ends, he says he intends to disappear from public life entirely. "When this is all done, you won't see me. I don't want to live a life in the public eye," he has said. Brittani, it seems, was always headed in the same direction. He just had to catch up.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: How Brittany Mahomes went from Whitehouse, Texas to Sports Illustrated swimsuit rookie without losing who she is
articles.summary: NFL News: Brittany Mahomes appeared in the 2024 Sports Illustrated Swimsuit issue as a rookie, shot on the beaches of Belize for the magazine's 60th anniversary.
articles.body: Brittany Mahomes appeared in the 2024 Sports Illustrated Swimsuit issue as a rookie, shot on the beaches of Belize for the magazine's 60th anniversary edition. For a lot of people, that felt like a celebrity flex, another moment from the NFL's most visible couple. But strip away the headlines and the Arrowhead Stadium cameras, and what you actually find is a woman who built something real long before Patrick Mahomes became a household name. Her path to that Mugler one-piece wasn't through the NFL. It ran through a soccer field in East Texas.How did Brittany Mahomes become famous before marrying Patrick Mahomes?Brittany grew up in Whitehouse, Texas, and by her senior year of high school was already turning heads as a forward, scoring 22 goals and earning Offensive MVP and All-East Texas honors. She was not chasing cameras. She was chasing a ball.At the University of Texas at Tyler, she became the first player in program history to record three hat tricks in a season. She graduated with a kinesiology degree, then spent a year playing professionally in Iceland before pivoting to fitness entrepreneurship. That's a genuinely full athletic biography, one that most people skipped reading because it didn't come with a Super Bowl ring attached to it.The irony is that when asked what would surprise her college-aged self most about her life today, she doesn't hesitate, and it isn't fame, three kids, or marrying her high school sweetheart that she mentions first. Her sense of self was formed before any of that arrived. That foundation matters, because everything she's built since has required her to hold onto it under real pressure.Why did Brittany Mahomes face so much online hate and how did she handle it?As Patrick's NFL career exploded and the Chiefs kept winning, the intensity of scrutiny on Brittany grew with it. Trolls criticized her for how she celebrated her husband's wins. She was called annoying, attention-seeking, fame-hungry. None of those accusations squared with the facts of who she actually was before any of this.She's been open about learning not to let haters get to her, but she's also made clear she's still human. When rude comments spiked, she didn't disappear. She pushed back directly, publicly, without apology. That consistency, showing up the same way whether she's getting praised or dragged, is what separates her from the WAG narrative people keep trying to write for her.Even a single Instagram like on a Donald Trump post spiralled into a full news cycle. Her response was characteristically blunt: "To be a hater as an adult, you have to have some deep-rooted issues you refuse to heal from childhood." Whether you agree with her politics or not, that's not a woman hiding behind a famous last name.What has Brittany Mahomes done to build her own legacy outside of the NFL?In 2020, when women's soccer was not yet the smart investment conversation it is today, Brittany joined the ownership group that brought an NWSL expansion team to Kansas City. Patrick joined two years later. The franchise is now valued at $325 million, the second most valuable team in the league, and CPKC Stadium opened in 2024 as the first purpose-built stadium for a professional women's sports team in the world.When Sports Illustrated named her a 2024 Swimsuit rookie, its editor-in-chief MJ Day described her as the founder of the world's first dedicated stadium for women's sports, someone whose journey had surpassed all expectations. That's not marketing language for a quarterback's wife. That's a legitimate sports business record.As for how Brittany herself processed it: "As a girl from Tyler, Texas, who only really knew sports, never in a million years did I think I'd be in the SI Swimsuit Issue. I'm just so grateful for this opportunity." There's no performance in that quote. It sounds like someone who genuinely didn't see it coming, because her reference point for her own life has always been the soccer field, not the celebrity circuit.That's the part people keep missing about Brittany Mahomes. The fame found her. She was already busy building something else.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Is Alberto Mendoza Fernando Mendoza’s brother? Inside the family connection behind Georgia Tech’s rising quarterback
articles.summary: NFL News: Alberto Mendoza arrived at Georgia Tech this season carrying a last name that college football fans already know well. His older brother Fernando Mend.
articles.body: Alberto Mendoza arrived at Georgia Tech this season carrying a last name that college football fans already know well. His older brother Fernando Mendoza won the Heisman Trophy last year at Indiana, then went first overall to the Las Vegas Raiders in the 2026 NFL Draft. Now Alberto, no longer playing second fiddle in Bloomington, is Georgia Tech's starting quarterback. The two are brothers, yes. But the real story runs deeper than that.Are Alberto and Fernando Mendoza actually brothers?Yes, they are. Both grew up in Miami, Florida, and both played quarterback at Christopher Columbus High School in Westchester before eventually sharing a backfield at Indiana University.Their father, Fernando Mendoza Sr., is a physician at Nicklaus Children's Hospital in Miami. Before medicine, he played alongside current Miami head coach Mario Cristobal at Columbus High School, then rowed at Brown University. In 1987, he won a gold medal at the Junior World Rowing Championships. Their mother Elsa, also from Miami, played tennis and earned two degrees. The household ran on discipline and competition. That much is obvious when you look at what both sons became.Fernando was first. He finished his high school career with 2,222 passing yards and 29 touchdowns, completing 67.5 percent of his throws. Alberto followed him and did one better, posting a 26-2 record as starter and winning back-to-back state championships in 2022 and 2023. Same school, same position, same family. Different paths to get there.The family also has a younger son, Max, who attended Columbus High but has set his sights on broadcasting rather than football.Why did Alberto Mendoza leave Indiana for Georgia Tech?Playing behind your Heisman-winning brother sounds like a dream setup, until you want to actually start.Alberto originally committed to James Madison University before switching to Indiana to play for coach Curt Cignetti. Fernando had already made his way to Bloomington from California, and the two ended up on the same roster. They became the first brothers in a decade to throw touchdown passes in the same game for one team.Fernando had a season that most quarterbacks never come close to. He completed 273 of 379 passes for 3,535 yards, threw 41 touchdowns against six interceptions, and added 440 rushing yards and seven scores on the ground. Indiana won the national championship. Fernando declared for the draft. He signed a four-year, fully guaranteed $57.27 million rookie contract with the Raiders.Alberto's numbers were solid for a backup. In nine games, he completed 18 of 24 passes for 286 yards, five touchdowns, and one interception, while adding 190 rushing yards and a score on the ground. But when Indiana brought in TCU transfer Josh Hoover to compete for the starting job, the writing was on the wall. Alberto transferred to Georgia Tech, where he is now the guy under center with no famous brother behind him.It is a fair question whether Alberto has lived in Fernando's shadow a little too long for anyone to evaluate him properly. Georgia Tech gives him a clean slate. This season will be the first real chance fans get to see what Alberto Mendoza is actually capable of when the last name is the only thing he is carrying.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: “I realized this boy is just a regular cool dude”: How Travis Kelce left an undrafted Chiefs rookie stunned with one unexpected gesture
articles.summary: NFL News: Travis Kelce has built a reputation as one of the Kansas City Chiefs’ biggest stars, but one of his most memorable moments with a teammate had nothing.
articles.body: Travis Kelce has built a reputation as one of the Kansas City Chiefs’ biggest stars, but one of his most memorable moments with a teammate had nothing to do with football. It happened in a training camp lunchroom in 2023, when an undrafted rookie found himself sitting alone with no familiar faces around him. Kelce noticed him, walked over and did something so ordinary that it caught the rookie completely off guard. For Izaiah Gathings, that small moment changed the way he saw the veteran tight end. Travis Kelce made an isolated rookie feel at homeGathings entered the Chiefs as an undrafted rookie in 2023 after spending time with the New York Jets. When he arrived at Kansas City’s training camp in St. Joseph, Missouri, he barely knew anyone on the roster. After one practice, he walked into the lunchroom, grabbed his food and sat by himself while looking at his phone.Then Kelce walked over. As Gathings later explained on his YouTube channel, he was eating quietly when he noticed two plates of food being placed beside him. Kelce then sat down and asked, “Yo what’s up with you, my boy. You straight?”For Gathings, the surprise came from more than the food. This was Travis Kelce, one of the biggest names in the NFL, choosing to sit beside an undrafted rookie he barely knew and have a normal conversation. The Kansas City Star reported the story on January 5, 2024, after Gathings shared the experience.Gathings admitted that he was stunned by how casually Kelce treated him. “Just imagine you sitting there eating your lunch and all of a sudden Travis Kelce comes up beside you and say, ‘Boy, you straight?’ And then proceeds to sit down and have a normal convo with me, like just a regular convo,” he said.That interaction stayed with Gathings because Kelce never made him feel like the new guy who had to prove himself before getting noticed. Instead, he simply pulled up a chair and talked to him.“At that moment right there with my boy Trav, I realized like bro is just a regular cool a** dude, bro,” Gathings said. “Funny as hell, like fun to be around. Bro is cool as hell.” Clyde Edwards-Helaire found the same support in a harder momentGathings was not the only young Chiefs player who felt Kelce’s support away from the field. Clyde Edwards-Helaire has spoken openly about how Kelce noticed when he was struggling with his mental health and became someone he could lean on.During The Pivot Podcast episode released on November 8, 2024, Edwards-Helaire described Kelce as a “big brother” and said, “I really look at him as a big brother and I needed somebody to lean on.” He also revealed that Kelce would check in on him and called him “GBC,” short for Good Brother Clyde.Months earlier, Edwards-Helaire had explained why Kelce's support stood out. “In a lot of those times kind of dealing with my mental health, it seemed like nobody else noticed,” he said. “And he did, you know?”Kelce later shared the podcast episode on X and called Edwards-Helaire “one of the strongest men I know.”Those moments show a side of his leadership that does not appear on the stat sheet. He notices people, especially teammates who might otherwise feel overlooked, and makes sure they know they are not alone.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Are You Prepared For the 2026 Football Tax This Season?
articles.summary: "The Football Tax feels like an investment. Every year, football asks fans for a little more, and every year, fans grumble. Every year, we pay it anyway." Th...
articles.body:
Every September, football fans get a bill. Not an actual bill, of course. Roger Goodell isn't mailing invoices to America just yet. But if you're a football fan, you know exactly what I'm talking about.

It's the annual Football Tax: the price we pay to consume the greatest television product this country has ever created. Every year, the games spread out a little more. Another streaming service joins the party. Another package gets added, and another app finds its way onto your television. Every year, fans swear they've reached their limit. Yet, every year, opening weekend arrives and we sign up anyway.

So, like I do every year, I wanted to figure out exactly what it costs to watch as much football as humanly possible in 2026. Not casually. I'm talking about the hardcore fan. The fan who wants every NFL game, every major college football game, Sunday Ticket , RedZone , conference championship games, playoff games and enough football to make family members question whether you're ever leaving the couch.

The answer is somewhere between $1,100 and $1,200. That's not cheap. It's also a tremendous amount of football.

The foundation for most football fans is YouTube TV. At $82.99 per month, it delivers CBS, FOX, NBC, ABC, ESPN, ESPN2, NFL Network, Big Ten Network, SEC Network, ACC Network and most of the channels that carry the games we care about every weekend.

Over the course of a five-month football season, that comes to about $415. For a lot of fans, that would be enough. But we're not talking about a lot of fans. We're talking about football people.

If you're serious about the NFL, Sunday Ticket remains one of the best products in sports television. Want to watch your favorite team after moving across the country? Sunday Ticket . Want to track playoff races around the league? Sunday Ticket . Want four games on the screen at once because your fantasy season is hanging by a thread? Sunday Ticket .

Returning customers currently pay about $378 for the season when bundled with YouTube TV.

Then comes RedZone , which at this point feels less like a channel and more like a lifestyle choice. Seven straight hours of touchdowns, highlights, fantasy points and Scott Hanson somehow speaking continuously without food, water or a substitute teacher. The Sports Plus package that includes RedZone runs another $10.99 per month, adding about $55 over the course of the season.

Thursday Night Football stays on Prime Video. Netflix is again part of the NFL landscape through its holiday games. Peacock continues to carry exclusive NFL inventory and remains important for both NFL and college football fans. None of these services are particularly expensive by themselves, but together, they become part of the Football Tax.

Prime Video costs about $15 per month. Peacock Premium sits around $13 per month. Netflix's standard plan runs about $18 per month. Over a five-month season, that's another $230 added to the tax.

Then there's college football, which somehow manages to be both easier and more complicated at the same time. The good news is that one service does most of the heavy lifting. The bad news is that college football rights have become as complicated as NIL.

The SEC lives on ESPN. The Big Ten is spread across FOX, CBS, NBC and Peacock. The ACC is heavily tied to ESPN and ABC. The challenge isn't finding the game. The challenge is remembering where the game lives each week.

For the deeply committed college football fan, Paramount+ is worth adding to the lineup because it provides streaming access to CBS content and helps fill in some of the remaining gaps. Depending on the package, you're looking at another $45 to $50 over the course of the season.

That puts the grand total at approximately $1,128 for the season based on those figures. With the final cost varying depending on the plans and promotions you choose.

Now, before you spit out your Bloody Mary, remember what you're buying.

NFL Sundays from September through January. College football Saturdays. Rivalry games. Playoff races. Conference championship games. The College Football Playoff, NFL playoffs, and the Super Bowl.

You're investing in hundreds of games and thousands of hours of programming. In an era when television shows disappear after one season, movies come and go in a weekend and streaming services constantly fight for your attention, football is still one of the few entertainment products that consistently lives up to the hype.

Every week brings another upset, another game-winning drive, another unbelievable finish. Also another reason to stay glued to the screen.

For all the complaints about streaming, subscriptions and rising costs, football has never been more accessible. Twenty years ago, if your team wasn't on local television, you were out of luck. Today, every NFL game and every major college football game is available somewhere.

The challenge isn't finding the game. The challenge is remembering whether it's on YouTube TV, Prime Video, Peacock, Netflix, Paramount+, ESPN or one of the other apps currently occupying space on your television.

Yes, the Football Tax is real. Most taxes feel like money disappearing. The Football Tax feels like an investment. Every year, football asks fans for a little more, and every year, fans grumble. Every year, we pay it anyway.

Then opening weekend arrives. RedZone fires up. College football takes over Saturday. The NFL owns Sunday. Suddenly, nobody is thinking about the bill anymore.

We're thinking about football. And that's the thing about the Football Tax. The bill may arrive in September.

articles.title: 1 Reason Every NFL Fanbase Should Have Hope for 2026 Season
articles.summary: Before reality hits in the opening week of the 2026 NFL season, there's still time for some optimism.
articles.body:
Before reality hits in the opening week of the 2026 NFL season, there's still time for some optimism.

Of course, every fanbase would like to see their team hoist the Lombardi Trophy on February 14 at SoFi Stadium, but what factors could contribute to that happening?

In discussing that, we can dive into recent trends, new acquisitions and career resumes.

Using the power of positivity, here's one sentence that provides optimism for every team ahead of the upcoming season.

Buffalo Bills: Head coach Joe Brady has reunited with DJ Moore, who averaged a career-high 18.1 yards per catch in the play-caller's Carolina Panthers offense in 2020.

Miami Dolphins: At 5'9", 195 pounds, De'Von Achane has shown he can be a workhorse running back and a quarterback's safety blanket, racking up 1,838 scrimmage yards (1,350 rushing and 488 receiving) and 12 touchdowns while averaging a whopping 5.7 yards per carry last season.

New England Patriots: Drake Maye is coming off an MVP-worthy year, and the Patriots significantly upgraded his wide receiver corps with the addition of three-time Pro Bowler A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs to help him navigate a much tougher schedule.

New York Jets: Geno Smith will play behind a far superior offensive line than the poorly coached, injury-riddled Las Vegas Raiders' unit that struggled to protect him while he took a league-high 55 sacks last season.

Baltimore Ravens: Since 2018, the Ravens have only missed the playoffs when their defense ranked worse than ninth in scoring, so it's worth noting that head coach Jesse Minter's Los Angeles Chargers defenses ranked No. 1 and No. 9 in points allowed over the last two years.

Cincinnati Bengals: Joe Burrow has rebounded from two injury-riddled seasons to win Comeback Player of the Year and can do it again to become the first player to earn the award three times.

Cleveland Browns: With complementary skill sets, wideouts Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion will make the Browns' aerial attack worth watching as they develop through their rookie campaign.

Pittsburgh Steelers: With his starting quarterback healthy for more than half a season—so excluding the 2020 and 2024 campaigns—head coach Mike McCarthy led the Dallas Cowboys to 12 wins.

Houston Texans: The Texans defense, which ranked within the top three in total yards, scoring, takeaways and first downs allowed last year, can lead this team on a deep playoff run with just marginal improvement on offense.

Indianapolis Colts: Daniel Jones recorded career highs in completion rate (68 percent), passing yards per game (238.5), QBR (63), and passer rating (100.2) in his first year under play-calling head coach Shane Steichen.

Jacksonville Jaguars: Along with the Super Bowl-contending Seattle Seahawks and New England Patriots, the Jaguars were one of three teams to field a top-eight scoring offense and defense last season.

Tennessee Titans: Cam Ward has yet to throw multiple interceptions in a career game, and he's tossed two touchdown passes in four of his last five outings.

Chicken equity? This may be the wildest jersey number trade yet

Denver Broncos: The Broncos' elite-level starting offensive line, featuring All-Pros Garett Bolles and Quinn Meinerz, remains intact for a third consecutive year, which is a strong positive for Bo Nix, who will look to build a rapport with new lead receiver Jaylen Waddle.

Kansas City Chiefs: Based on the fact that the Chiefs offense has ranked 15th or worse in scoring since offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy's departure in 2023, his return and intense coaching style are exactly what the Chiefs need on that side of the ball.

Las Vegas Raiders: After leading the Seattle Seahawks' third-ranked scoring offense last season, new Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak has earned the trust that he can get the most out of All-Pro tight end Brock Bowers and 2025 first-rounder Ashton Jeanty.

Los Angeles Chargers: Given that offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel immediately elevated quarterback Tua Tagovailoa in Miami, two-time Pro Bowler Justin Herbert should be in line for a career year in the Chargers' new offense.

Dallas Cowboys: As a well-traveled 34-year-old pro coach who's been part of three different coaching staffs that developed top-nine scoring defenses, defensive coordinator Christian Parker could be a difference-maker for a unit that allowed the most points last season.

New York Giants: Despite being noncommittal about his Week 1 status, Pro Bowl wideout Malik Nabers shed his non-contract jersey at practice early last week, which is a positive sign for his availability.

Philadelphia Eagles: New offensive coordinator Sean Mannion will carry over play design concepts from head coaches Sean McVay and Matt LaFleur, who emphasize the ground attack, which is a signal for a heavy dose of All-Pro running back Saquon Barkley behind a high-level offensive line.

Washington Commanders: Jayden Daniels must love that the Commanders signed the league's best No. 2 receiver , Stefon Diggs, to complement Terry McLaurin and bolster a passing attack that ranked 24th in total yards last season.

Chicago Bears: Although Chicago traded wideout DJ Moore to the Buffalo Bills, Caleb Williams is poised to be the Bears' first quarterback to throw for 4,000-plus yards in his second year under head coach Ben Johnson, who's fielded a top-10 passing offense in all four of his seasons as a play-caller.

Detroit Lions: The Lions will only go on the road once between their Week 6 bye mid-October and their Week 12 Thanksgiving matchup against the Bears, and it's to face the rebuilding Miami Dolphins in Week 9.

Green Bay Packers: With running back Josh Jacobs on the Commissioner's Exempt List, quarterback Jordan Love can show he's a legitimate Pro Bowl-caliber player following two years in which the Packers have ranked within the bottom six in pass attempts.

Minnesota Vikings: Kyler Murray is the Vikings' most dynamic starting quarterback in head coach Kevin O'Connell's tenure, which will allow him to open up his playbook.

Atlanta Falcons: Two-time Coach of the Year Kevin Stefanski had a winning record of 37-30 in his first four years with the Cleveland Browns, which is a sliver of hope that he can turn a mediocre Falcons squad into a legitimate playoff contender right away.

Carolina Panthers: The Panthers offense can see exponential growth with 2025 Offensive Rookie of the Year Tetairoa McMillan playing with a bulked-up body and third-year running back Jonathon Brooks' return from a second torn ACL.

New Orleans Saints: Travis Etienne Jr. can contend for the rushing title behind an offensive line that features two recent first-round tackles, two-time Pro Bowl center Erik McCoy and free-agent acquisition David Edwards, who helped lead the charge on the ground for 2025 rushing champion James Cook last season.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers: Entering the final year of his contract, Baker Mayfield is in a familiar situation of betting on himself , which has worked out favorably for him in the past.

Arizona Cardinals: The offensive quartet of All-Pro tight end Trey McBride, rookie Jeremiyah Love and wideouts Marvin Harrison Jr. and Michael Wilson is worth watching under new offensive-minded head coach Mike LaFleur.

Los Angeles Rams: Under football mastermind Sean McVay, the Rams could be on the cusp of world domination with Aaron Donald coming out of retirement to join forces with two-time Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett and the team's No. 1 scoring offense from last season.

San Francisco 49ers: Rookie second-round wideout De'Zhaun Stribling can provide the youthful vigor the 49ers' vertical passing attack needs with seasoned veterans Mike Evans and George Kittle coming off an injury-shortened season.

Seattle Seahawks: Led by All-Pro wideout Jaxon Smith-Njigba, the real deal (not a fluke), Sam Darnold and head coach Mike Macdonald's stingy defense, the reigning champions aren't fading away anytime soon.

Maurice Moton covers the NFL for Bleacher Report. You can follow him on Twitter @MoeMoton .

articles.title: Cleveland Browns' Biggest Team Needs and Trade Targets Entering the 2026 NFL Season
articles.summary: The Cleveland Browns enter the 2026 NFL season with more questions than answers.
articles.body:
The Cleveland Browns enter the 2026 NFL season with more questions than answers.

Todd Monken is entering his first year as a head coach. They have a desperate need at quarterback and the passer of the future might not even be on the roster.

The defense will attempt to move forward without one of the league's best players in Myles Garrett.

The new campaign will be about finding out the answers to these questions. That doesn't mean they won't be looking to improve the roster, though. That's still Andrew Berry's primary job.

Here, we'll take a look at the team's biggest needs and the trade targets who could address them.

Deshaun Watson, Shedeur Sanders, Dillon Gabriel, Taylen Green.

The Deshaun Watson era has brought nothing but woe to the Cleveland Browns. Yet, the franchise is set to give him another shot. It should be his last. The fact that he was named the starter doesn't speak very highly of Monken's evaluation of Sanders, either. Ultimately, the solution at quarterback doesn't appear to be on the roster at this point.

The answer might not be on the roster, but the Browns don't seem likely to find one on the trade block either. They kept four quarterbacks going into the season with Gabriel going to the injured reserve to start the year.

However, Kyler Murray's emergence as Minnesota's starter raises questions about J.J. McCarthy's future with the Vikings. Mac Jones may have played his way into another opportunity to compete for a starting job after serving as Brock Purdy's backup.

The Eagles added Andy Dalton in the offseason and also drafted Cole Payton in the fifth round. They might be willing to part with intriguing backup Tanner McKee.

Denzel Ward, Tyson Campbell, Myles Harden, Noah Igbinoghene, Mekhi Blackmon, Toriano Pride Jr.

Ward showed he can still be a shutdown corner heading into his age-29 season. But he's also never played a full season in his career. Tyson Campbell played well after being traded to Cleveland last season, but he gave up 22 touchdowns in five seasons with Jacksonville. Myles Harden gave up a passer rating of 120.0 in the slot last season. All of the depth players are newcomers with something to prove.

Kristian Fulton, Riley Moss, Michael Carter II

The Chiefs loaded up on cornerbacks after trading away Trent McDuffie this offseason. Kristian Fulton could be the odd man out of the rotation with the first-round pick Mansoor Delane and Nohl Williams starting. He would bring more experience to the table.

Riley Moss is a name to keep an eye on as the season gets rolling. He's in a contract year and the Broncos are already paying up for Patrick Surtain II.

Michael Carter II would give them a veteran slot option to push Harden. He's stuck at the bottom of a deep secondary in Philadelphia.

Harold Fannin Jr., Blake Whiteheart, Carsen Ryan

Monken earned the Cleveland job, in part, because of what he did with the Baltimore Ravens offense last season.

The Browns were first in 12 personnel usage last season, and Monken utilized it at the third-highest rate . That was easy to do with Isaiah Likely and Mark Andrews. Harold Fannin Jr. was a bright spot for the offense in his rookie season.

There isn't any proven depth on the roster now.

Evan Engram, Theo Johnson, Quintin Morris

Engram is the biggest name who could be available on the trade block. However, the financial realities of his contract don't match up with the production that he has given Denver.

The more realistic path toward improving the room would be targeting a better fit whose circumstances could lead to him being dealt.

Theo Johnson has the tools to make a leap, but John Harbaugh brought Isaiah Likely with him to the Giants. Quintin Morris is a blocking tight end who could take some of the dirty work off Fannin's plate.

Chicken equity? This may be the wildest jersey number trade yet

Jared Verse, Isaiah McGuire, Derek Barnett, Sam Williams

Because replacing Myles Garrett is hard. It became even harder when Alex Wright, fresh off a three-year, $33 million contract extension in November, suffered a ruptured Achilles in practice. The Browns have since added Derek Barnett and Sam Williams off waivers. That isn't likely to be enough to get them through the season with a viable pass rush.

The Browns shouldn't be taking too big of a swing here. There's still money invested in Wright and they'll have to hope he can come back from a devastating injury next season.

A 33-year-old veteran like Bud Dupree shouldn't cost too much and the Chargers might want to clear more snaps for rookie Akheem Mesidor.

The other tactic would be targeting a former first-round pick on the final year of his deal. Felix Anudike-Uzomah hasn't broken out in Kansas City and they already declined his fifth-year option. A change of scenery could help.

articles.title: Bold Trade Predictions Before the 2026 NFL Season Kicks Off
articles.summary: With the preseason complete, initial 53-man rosters set and early free agency a distant memory, NFL teams largely know what sort of rosters they're carrying into Week 1.
articles.body:
With the preseason complete, initial 53-man rosters set and early free agency a distant memory, NFL teams largely know what sort of rosters they're carrying into Week 1.

Many of those rosters will look different by midseason, though, and trades will be a big part of the equation.

Some teams will look to the trade market early in the year to fill remaining roster holes, while others will look to swing deals after key injuries arise. Yet other teams will look to sell off pieces while looking ahead to the future and a loaded 2027 draft.

This year's trade window won't close until November 10, but it's never too early to survey the landscape and make a few bold predictions. That's precisely what we'll do here by diving into seven bold-but-realistic scenarios that would change the NFL picture in 2026.

The Pittsburgh Steelers would certainly prefer to keep starting cornerback Joey Porter Jr. However, their desire to delay contract talks with him may force Pittsburgh to consider a trade instead.

ESPN's Jeremy Fowler wrote the following on Wednesday:

"Sources say the Steelers' lack of a formal offer for weeks sent the clear message to Porter that they would like him to play out the final year of his rookie contract, which prompted him to consider the possibility of a trade or sitting out for an extended period."

If things get to a point where the Steelers don't believe they can keep Porter, flipping him for a high 2027 pick will become an option for them. Aaron Rodgers isn't the future at quarterback, and while Pittsburgh may hope that either Will Howard or Drew Allar can be, it wouldn't hurt to have a pair of first-round picks in what is expected to be a QB-heavy draft.

The Detroit Lions, meanwhile, could be prompted to make an aggressive move for a defensive difference-maker like Porter.

After missing the playoffs in 2025, the Lions are undoubtedly eager to get back to the top of the NFC North mountain. They could also use a new starter after parting with 2024 first-round pick Terrion Arnold this offseason.

Cardinals Get: Conditional 2027 4th-Round Pick

Though he was the topic of trade speculation early in the offseason, the Arizona Cardinals are reportedly uninterested in moving pass-rusher Josh Sweat.

"The Cardinals are telling interested teams they aren't planning to trade Sweat, and I believe that to be true," ESPN's Dan Graziano wrote.

The caveat here is that, as Graziano noted, "no team has won or lost any games yet."

Arizona will likely change its stance on trading players if and when it becomes clear that it can't contend in 2026—or if it becomes obvious that rookie quarterback Carson Beck isn't a franchise savior.

Sweat will turn 30 next offseason and looms as a potential 2027 cap casualty. Moving him for quality draft capital would make sense. Giving up a conditional pick that could become a Day-2 selection for Sweat would be logical for a contender like the Chicago Bears.

Chicago still needs a consistent edge presence opposite Montez Sweat, and it could acquire one by doing a deal with the Cardinals.

Bills Get: Conditional 2027 5th-Round Pick

The San Francisco 49ers already have some question marks at wide receiver. Though they did bring back Deebo Samuel and sign Mike Evans, they also lost Jauan Jennings in free agency and lost Ricky Pearsall to season-ending injured reserve (PCL).

The 49ers will rely heavily on aging wideouts and rookie De'Zhaun Stribling , and they could afford to add some extra depth to their receiver room. Buffalo Bills receiver Keon Coleman, meanwhile, could use a fresh start.

Coleman, the 33rd overall pick in the 2024 draft, hasn't developed into a reliable go-to receiver in Buffalo. He wasn't always even part of the game plan in 2025, though he does have a supporter in former offensive coordinator and current head coach Joe Brady.

"I was one of the ones that stood on the table for Keon Coleman, and I believe in Keon Coleman," Brady said, per ESPN's Alaina Getzenberg .

At some point, Brady will have to place more importance on results than his belief in a former draft pick. If Coleman continues to struggle, Brady will have to create more opportunities for 2025 free-agent addition Joshua Palmer and rookie Skyler Bell .

A trade could help create those opportunities while giving Coleman a new chance in Kyle Shanahan's offense.

Chicken equity? This may be the wildest jersey number trade yet

While J.J. McCarthy wasn't released or traded ahead of the cuts deadline, it still feels like his time with the Minnesota Vikings is running out—even if the team says otherwise.

"J.J. McCarthy's role is to continue to develop, to improve and to support his teammates," GM Nolan Teasley said, per ESPN's Kevin Seifert . "And he's done an excellent job of that from the moment that I've been here and, from my understanding, since he walked through the door."

The Vikings were quick to name free-agent addition Kyler Murray as their starter, and they have a veteran backup in Carson Wentz. While continuing to develop McCarthy is an option, Minnesota may want to rip off the proverbial Band-Aid and move on from him.

The problem is that McCarthy doesn't have much of a trade market after struggling to stay healthy and largely playing poorly over his first two seasons.

The Los Angeles Chargers are one team that might be willing to take a chance on McCarthy. Los Angeles has its starting quarterback in Justin Herbert, but it has a less-experienced backup in Trey Lance, who is also on a one-year deal.

Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh was McCarthy's coach at Michigan, and he could be interested in developing his former starter as a long-term backup in L.A.

While this isn't a trade that would impact the starting lineup of either the Vikings or the Chargers, it would officially bring an end to the McCarthy experiment in Minnesota.

While the New England Patriots just represented the AFC in Super Bowl LX, they are still an emerging team. New England has holes on its roster that it should be looking to fill with younger long-term talent.

One of the Patriots' biggest weaknesses is their pass rush. While New England did sign Dre'Month Jones and use a second-round pick on Illinois' Gabe Jacas , it also recorded just 34 sacks as a team last season.

If the Patriots' pass rush struggles again early in 2026, don't be shocked if they go chasing sack artists on the trade market—and given their desire to avoid the dreaded Super Bowl hangover, don't be surprised if they get a little desperate.

Earlier in the offseason, the New York Giants were listening to offers for 2022 first-round pick Kayvon Thibodeaux, who is entering the final year of his rookie deal. However, they couldn't find a buyer at their desired price.

According to Dan Duggan of The Athletic, the Giants had conversations with the New Orleans Saints during draft weekend, though their asking price of a second-round pick was something the Saints weren't willing to meet.

The Patriots, who are looking to build rather than rebuild, might be more eager to meet New York's demands, even if a trade for Thibodeaux would require a new contract.

Raiders Get: 2027 1st-Round Pick, 2028 1st-Round Pick, Edge Rashan Gary

The Dallas Cowboys have taken an aggressive approach to rebuilding their defense this offseason, and franchise owner Jerry Jones has stated that he may not be finished making moves.

"A top pick is expendable this year to add somebody meaningful that would help us now," Jones said in July, per The Athletic's Jon Machota .

Jones has also made it clear that Dallas never closed the door on trading for Las Vegas Raiders pass-rusher Maxx Crosby.

"We did not walk away. That's about all there is to say," Jones said, per Machota.

While the Cowboys have since added Von Miller to their pass-rushing rotation, it wouldn't be a shock to see them make another run at Crosby closer to the trade deadline.

If Dallas looks like a formidable playoff contender by November, trading valuable draft capital—along with a proven player like Rashan Gary, who was acquired via trade early in the offseason—to get Crosby could be the sort of all-in move that Jones believes will get him to the Super Bowl.

The Raiders seem content to keep Crosby after their offseason trade with the Baltimore Ravens fell through. However, they could revisit the idea of flipping the 29-year-old if they're struggling to compete in late October.

After taking Fernando Mendoza No. 1 overall, Las Vegas won't be in the market for a quarterback in next year's draft. However, it will be looking for long-term pieces to put around Mendoza. Trading Crosby, who could be past his prime by the time the Raiders are ready to contend, could get Las Vegas a very strong return.

Browns Get: Conditional 2027 7th-Round Pick, QB Tua Tagovailoa

The Atlanta Falcons have yet to name a starting quarterback, which doesn't bode particularly well for free-agent addition Tua Tagovailoa. Atlanta signed the former Miami Dolphins starter to compete with 2024 first-round pick Michael Penix Jr., but Penix hasn't been able to do much competing while recovering from a torn ACL.

According to NFL Network's Cameron Wolfe , the Falcons' plan is to start Penix "eventually."

Atlanta also has Cooper Rush and undrafted free agent Jack Strand in its quarterback room. However, Tagovailoa and Penix are most likely the only quarterbacks that the new regime views as potential long-term options. If and when those two fail to impress, the Falcons will probably begin evaluating 2027 quarterback prospects.

Along the way, the Falcons could look to add another potential bridge quarterback by trading for Cleveland Browns third-stringer Dillon Gabriel. The Oregon product started six games as a rookie in 2025, had a strong preseason finale last month, and has experience in Kevin Stefanski's offense.

Gabriel will open the season on injured reserve with a back injury but has been designated to return. The Falcons could acquire the 2025 third-rounder by surrendering a Day-3 pick and by giving the Browns another reclamation project at quarterback to audition.

This isn't a trade that would rock the playoff picture, but it would impact two teams desperate for a franchise quarterback.

articles.summary: The Buffalo Bills' latest quest to win their first Super Bowl is on the horizon, and the roster is quite robust entering the 2026 campaign.
articles.body:
The Buffalo Bills' latest quest to win their first Super Bowl is on the horizon, and the roster is quite robust entering the 2026 campaign.

That explains why they're the AFC favorite to reach Super Bowl LXI, but it doesn't mean there aren't weak spots.

On the brink of Week 1, let's go over the four key areas of need on the roster while looking at potential trade targets at each position in the coming weeks and months.

Christian Benford, Maxwell Hairston, Dee Alford, Davison Igbinosun, Jordan Hancock

Buffalo has a capable top trio in Christian Benford, Maxwell Hairston and Dee Alford, who gives the defense a reliable option in the nickel role.

The team should expect Hairston to develop in Year 2, but the depth chart could become vulnerable if his progress stalls or injuries strike.

Davison Igbinosun is a second-round rookie, while Jordan Hancock is realistically more of a safety who was limited as a fifth-round rookie in 2025.

Deonte Banks, Asante Samuel Jr., Kelee Ringo

Banks has shown flashes of the talent that made him a first-round pick, but he has struggled to establish consistency with the Giants. A change of scenery could give him an opportunity to rebuild his value as a depth option in Buffalo.

Samuel is a proven veteran on a cheap one-year deal in Pittsburgh, but the cornerback-rich Steelers could bail on that if they aren't getting much use out of him or they find themselves selling ahead of the deadline.

Ringo is a natural perimeter cover man who is buried on Philadelphia's depth chart entering a walk year.

Terrel Bernard, Dorian Williams, Kaleb Elarms-Orr, Joe Andreessen

The group has depth, particularly with rookie Elarms-Orr shining this summer and Shaq Thompson on the practice squad.

Still, Buffalo is expected to use 3-4 looks often, and Bernard and Williams project as replacement-level starters as the team moves on from the Matt Milano era.

Injuries are also a concern for both starters.

Pace is heading into a contract year in Minnesota, where he may be falling out of favor. He hasn't been himself since an awesome 2023 rookie season, but the ceiling remains quite high and a new setting could help.

Queen is another Pittsburgh veteran in a contract year who could become a trade piece for the Steelers if they fall out of playoff contention early.

Ed Oliver, Deone Walker, T.J. Sanders, Greg Gaines, Landon Jackson, DeWayne Carter

Oliver is solid when healthy, while Sanders and Carter offer capable interior support and Jackson provides developmental help off the edge.

Walker has promise on the interior but remains a work in progress, while the 30-year-old Gaines is not a player Buffalo should have to rely on heavily if injuries strike.

This unit is fine for now, but that could change quickly with an injury or unexpected slump.

Karl Brooks, Dante Stills, Harrison Phillips

Brooks is a rotational piece in Green Bay who may be losing ground in a crowded defensive-line group as he enters the final year of his rookie deal. He would make sense as a rental to bolster Buffalo's interior defensive-line depth if injuries thin the unit.

Stills is in a similar spot with the Cardinals, where he might not be part of the future beyond 2026.

Meanwhile, if the Jets find themselves struggling, it could make sense for Buffalo to attempt to bring back the 30-year-old Phillips amid a walk year.

Chicken equity? This may be the wildest jersey number trade yet

DJ Moore, Khalil Shakir, Keon Coleman, Joshua Palmer, Skyler Bell

Many would argue wide receiver is not a need, and it barely makes this list after the addition of Moore.

That said, Moore is 29 and saw his yardage numbers drop off sharply in his final couple seasons with the Bears.

There's decent depth beyond that, but they're only keeping five players.

In the case of Dell, we're thinking of a scenario in which he returns to health but finds himself out of favor in a receiving corps that also features Nico Collins, Jaylin Noel and the incoming Kayshon Boutte.

It might be tough to convince the Raiders to move Tucker, but he's a speed demon in a contract year who could put this offense over the top with the right supporting cast.

It's possible Las Vegas will shift its focus to Jalen Nailor, Jack Bech and the tight ends and take something for Tucker before the deadline.

articles.body:
The "NFL Top 100 Players" is an annual NFL offseason tradition. There are a few names from the Kansas City Chiefs expected to make the cut, but there are also many opponents featured in this year's rankings. Player No. 6 is a player they are scheduled to face this coming season.

McCaffrey started all 17 games for the 49ers in 2025, finishing with 311 carries for 1,202 rushing yards and ten rushing touchdowns to go with 102 receptions for 924 receiving yards and seven receiving touchdowns. He won the Comeback Player of the Year award at the NFL Honors ceremony.

articles.title: College football (mostly) moves out of the courtroom and onto the field
articles.summary: And on the third day of the ninth month in the year 2026 of our Savant and Savior Curt Cignetti, the college football gods mercifully said, “Let there be football.”
articles.body: And on the third day of the ninth month in the year 2026 of our Savant and Savior Curt Cignetti, the college football gods mercifully said, “Let there be football.” Goodbye injunctions and hello interceptions. Out with TROs and in with RPOs. Take a hike, local judges and make room for the line judges. An exhausting, head-spinning and often downright silly offseason is officially over after college football really kicked off on Thursday (after the always bizarre Week 0 last weekend). The machinations of the long break were replaced with the one thing that no one – despite serious efforts – can screw up: the football. It is undefeated, a reliable constant that rarely fails to deliver. It is a beautifully unscripted four-act drama that plays out over and over and draws us back to the tailgate grill like shot-gunning, beer-starved lemmings. Last season, Bill Belichick was terrible and Vanderbilt was good. Lane Kiffin’s chaotic departure from Ole Miss gave way to an epic playoff quarterfinal showdown between the team he jilted and Georgia. The upheaval of NIL overload had no chance against the exuberance of Fernando Mendoza. Indiana, winners of nothing, shellacked Alabama, winners of everything. And at the end of it all, a euphoric fan base, tipsy with its sudden reversal of fortune, belted out a 1976 Abba song in South Florida. And now here we are, a blank slate in front of us, with all of the promise it brings. No one is more optimistic than a fan of a yet-to-be-defeated, 0-0 team firing up the grill for the first time in months. It’s part of our very American psyche, this eternal hope of college football. Nowhere in the world do nonprofessionals (strictly speaking) merit the attention that the college football player here does. Freddy, the delightful World Cup fan from Germany who found his way to the US, was so wowed by the largesse of the college football stadiums and towns he visited on side trips, he’s now mapped out a fall football Saturday tour. If you think about it, it makes no sense. Eight of the top 10 largest stadiums in the world sit on college campuses, but college teams are far more regionalized than NFL squads. They draw from fervent alumni bases and students, compared with the endless suburban sprawl of a pro franchise. There are, for example, 800,000 living Penn State alumni and 1.5 million people living in Philly. With the addition of new west side stands that sit one step below the sun, Beaver Stadium now holds 109,000 compared to just 67,000 at the Eagles’ Lincoln Financial Field. The draw is, in part, the hoopla and traditions. It’s screaming “Go to hell, LSU,” at the end of the national anthem at Ole Miss games, long before Kiffin arrived, and changing the words to “Dixieland Delight” in Tuscaloosa. It’s Virginia Tech’s “Enter Sandman” and Wisconsin’s “Jump Around.” It’s the marching bands and the tailgating and the chance to be 20 again. Where else, after all, but at one’s alma mater can a 40-year-old do a keg stand to rousing applause? And despite the alleged game protectors’ attempts to destroy it by shattering geographic boundaries, canceling rivalries, ignoring warning signs and generally existing as ostriches crossed with peacocks, the conference commissioners and college presidents and TV execs can’t kill the feeling college football conjures. Big Ten consistency, SEC chaos What’s interesting, though, is that the disruptors might be killing their own shot at their very own golden goose. Chaos fatigue isn’t the only side dish being served with the recent rash of court orders; chaos consequences appear to be on a platter as well. The Big Ten has won the last three national titles via three different teams (Indiana, Michigan and Ohio State). This year two of its schools, Ohio State and Oregon, debut atop the polls, with defending champion Indiana clocking in at No. 6. Certainly, that’s a flex of the league’s pocketbook. Backed by its media-rights deal that helped generate some $1.47 billion in revenues last year, rich donors and coast-to-coast conference spread, the Big Ten is swimming in it. But if money alone could buy you a national title, wouldn’t Texas have a few more by now? No, along with more money, what the Big Ten seemingly has going for it is less mayhem (the regular occurrences in Ann Arbor notwithstanding). The coaches may not be linking arms over a fire and toasting s’mores, but they are not spewing bile when they say each other’s names, either. Kevin Warren did not engender a lot of love before leaving for the NFL, but he left his successor, Tony Petitti, a strong foundation on which to build. In a college athletics world standing atop a pile of quicksand, the Big Ten has stability. Consider: On August 25, the league passed a rule banning NFL players from playing for their teams. The next day, the SEC did the same. The Big Ten has moved along with nary a peep. The SEC went to the lawyers, got dissed by the lawyers and then threatened to exile one of its members (LSU) for its refusal to play by the conference’s rule. On Thursday, the SEC sued LSU over it, with Lane Kiffin as one of the co-defendants. The Tigers will play Clemson this weekend. No one seems to care much about the game. Similarly, at SEC Media Day, commissioner Greg Sankey intimated that frustration might someday lead to a breakaway from the NCAA. His words were, to be fair, taken a bit out of context. He was answering a direct question, not making a threat, but it came off that way, anyway. A week later, Petitti clarified the mess, explaining that, if things didn’t settle down then maybe they’d need a path to conference-based rules. None of this is exactly new. The SEC’s very identity is based on its audacity. The “It Just Means More” slogan is at once arrogant and entirely accurate. This is the league, remember, where a man (Harvey Updyke) confessed to poisoning the trees at Auburn on a radio show after Alabama lost to the Tigers, and a coach (Jackie Sherrill at Mississippi State) castrated a bull to motivate his squad. The SEC is not unlike its schools’ sorority rush: A fever-pitched dash of delirious disorder ginned up on hairspray and fake tans, with the lone goal to be voted most popular. But chaos comes with a price, and while “distractions” are often either easy crutches or a straw man for coaches to lean on, the league’s inability to concentrate on the task at hand seems to be catching up with it. While the SEC flails about amid coaching disruption - six new head coaches this year and nine since 2024 – lawsuits, roster manipulation and court orders, the Big Ten has been comparatively steady and drama-free. And they have the trophies to show for it. Way back in the 1930s, the Big Ten won four titles in a row – to tell you how long ago that really was, Minnesota won three of them – but no league has gone four-for-four with four different title-winning teams in the modern era. Oregon (preseason No. 2), Washington (No. 17), Penn State (No. 18), and Iowa (No. 22) would like to make history. Which, of course sounds outlandish. Except isn’t that what college football is all about in September? Indiana, after all, started the season ranked 20th last year.
